Web appendix H: Expectimax normative benchmarking

We benchmark observed LLM behavior against a normative Expectimax decision-tree policy. Expectimax approximates the decision-theoretic solution to a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) under resource scarcity (Russell, 2010). By recursively computing the Expected Value of Information (EVI) for each available tool call, the algorithm identifies the point at which the marginal informational benefit of inspecting an additional attribute no longer justifies the compounding financial search cost.

The shopping task

The decision environment casts the surrogate consumer in an electronic retailing choice task over a set of alternatives 𝒥={1,…,J}\mathcal{J}=\{1,\dots,J\}. The surrogate consumer is delegated to select a single alternative j∗∈𝒥j^{*}\in\mathcal{J} on behalf of a human consumer. The human consumer will subsequently purchase Q=5Q=5 units (bags) of the selected product.

Information acquisition is operationalized through discrete tool invocations. The surrogate consumer begins in an uninformative state where product attributes are occluded behind closed cells. Revealing an attribute cell incurs an explicit financial penalty c∈{$0.00,$0.01,$0.10,$1.00,$10.00}c\in\{\$0.00,\$0.01,\$0.10,\$1.00,\$10.00\} for Study 1 and c∈{$0.00,$0.01,$0.10,$1.00,$50.00}c\in\{\$0.00,\$0.01,\$0.10,\$1.00,\$50.00\} for Study 2, charged to the delegating consumer. Submitting a final choice incurs zero cost.

Objective function

A central question in benchmarking information acquisition is how non-monetary physical attributes (product weight in ounces) trade off against monetary search penalties (dollars). In our formulation, this exchange rate is derived from the economics of unit-price minimization.

When alternative jj is chosen, the human consumer incurs two financial costs: the purchase cost of the goods (Q⋅PjQ\cdot P_{j}) and the cumulative tool fees accrued during search (CtoolC_{\text{tool}}). In return, the consumer receives a total product volume of Q⋅WjQ\cdot W_{j} ounces. The net cost per ounce delivered to the consumer is:

Effective Unit Cost=Total Dollar CostTotal Ounces Delivered=Q⋅Pj+CtoolQ⋅Wj=(Pj+CtoolQ)​1Wj\text{Effective Unit Cost}=\frac{\text{Total Dollar Cost}}{\text{Total Ounces Delivered}}=\frac{Q\cdot P_{j}+C_{\text{tool}}}{Q\cdot W_{j}}=\left(P_{j}+\frac{C_{\text{tool}}}{Q}\right)\frac{1}{W_{j}}

where Q=5Q=5 is the purchase volume and Ctool​(s)=∑k∈inspected​(s)ckC_{\text{tool}}(s)=\sum_{k\in\text{inspected}(s)}c_{k} is the total financial cost incurred across all inspect_cell invocations executed to reach information state ss. PjP_{j} is the net price per bag. In Study 1, Pj=Dollarsj+0.01×CentsjP_{j}=\text{Dollars}_{j}+0.01\times\text{Cents}_{j}. In Study 2, Pj=ListPricej×(1−Discountj100)P_{j}=\text{ListPrice}_{j}\times\left(1-\frac{\text{Discount}_{j}}{100}\right). WjW_{j} is the net product weight in ounces.

Under partial information, price and weight are independently distributed across alternatives in the market prior. The expected effective unit cost of selecting alternative jj at state ss is:

𝔼⁡[Effective Unit Cost​(j)∣s]=(𝔼⁡[Pj∣s]+Ctool​(s)Q)⋅𝔼⁡[1Wj|s]\mathbb{E}\left[\text{Effective Unit Cost}(j)\mid s\right]=\left(\mathbb{E}[P_{j}\mid s]+\frac{C_{\text{tool}}(s)}{Q}\right)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{W_{j}}\;\Bigg|\;s\right]

Because the planner maximizes utility, terminal choice value is defined as the negative of the expected effective unit cost:

𝒰choose(j,s)=−(𝔼[Pj∣s]+Ctool​(s)Q)⋅𝔼[1Wj|s]\mathcal{U}_{\text{choose}}(j,s)=-\left(\mathbb{E}[P_{j}\mid s]+\frac{C_{\text{tool}}(s)}{Q}\right)\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{W_{j}}\;\Bigg|\;s\right]

This specification eliminates arbitrary subjective exchange rates. The monetary penalty of search (CtoolC_{\text{tool}}) is amortized directly across the 5-bag purchase quantity (Ctool/QC_{\text{tool}}/Q), establishing a dollar-for-ounce valuation that governs the optimal search threshold.

An information state ss is defined as a tuple of length J×KJ\times K, where JJ is the number of alternatives and KK is the number of attributes per alternative:

s=(v1,1,…,vj,k,…,vJ,K),vj,k∈𝒟k∪{None}s=\Big(v_{1,1},\dots,v_{j,k},\dots,v_{J,K}\Big),\quad v_{j,k}\in\mathcal{D}_{k}\cup\{\text{None}\}

where 𝒟k\mathcal{D}_{k} is the empirical domain of attribute kk, and None indicates that the attribute has not been inspected.

At each turn, the legal action space 𝒜⁡(s)\mathcal{A}(s) comprises two mutually exclusive subsets:

  1. 1.

    Reveal actions, 𝒜reveal​(s)={(reveal,j,k)∣sj,k=None}\mathcal{A}_{\text{reveal}}(s)=\{(\text{reveal},j,k)\mid s_{j,k}=\text{None}\}, which inspect an unobserved cell.

  2. 2.

    Choose actions, 𝒜choose​(s)={(choose,j)∣j∈𝒥}\mathcal{A}_{\text{choose}}(s)=\{(\text{choose},j)\mid j\in\mathcal{J}\}, which terminate search and submit a purchase.

Priors

Prior distributions are based on empirical instant coffee attributes collected from Walmart.com. Whole dollars (𝒟dollars\mathcal{D}_{\text{dollars}}) are 25 discrete values spanning $0\$0 to $53\$53 (M=$15.96M=\$15.96). Fractional cents (𝒟cents\mathcal{D}_{\text{cents}}) are 45 discrete values spanning 0​¢0\textcent to 99​¢99\textcent (M=52.93​¢M=52.93\textcent). Product weight (𝒟weight\mathcal{D}_{\text{weight}}) are 57 continuous values spanning 0.42​ oz0.42\text{ oz} to 71.99​ oz71.99\text{ oz} (M=10.33​ ozM=10.33\text{ oz}). List price (𝒟list_price\mathcal{D}_{\text{list\_price}}) are 63 continuous values spanning $0.92\$0.92 to $53.84\$53.84 (M=$11.87M=\$11.87). For discount percentage (𝒟discount\mathcal{D}_{\text{discount}}), we assume a discrete uniform distribution 𝒰​{0,40}\mathcal{U}\{0,40\} in 5% increments (M=20.0%M=20.0\%).

Prior expectations for unobserved attributes are precomputed over their respective empirical supports:

𝔼⁡[Dollars]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\text{Dollars}] =1|𝒟dollars|​∑d∈𝒟dollarsd,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{dollars}}|}\sum_{d\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{dollars}}}d, 𝔼⁡[Cents]\displaystyle\quad\mathbb{E}[\text{Cents}] =1|𝒟cents|​∑c∈𝒟centsc,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{cents}}|}\sum_{c\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{cents}}}c,
𝔼⁡[ListPrice]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\text{ListPrice}] =1|𝒟list_price|​∑p∈𝒟list_pricep,\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{list\_price}}|}\sum_{p\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{list\_price}}}p, 𝔼⁡[Discount]\displaystyle\quad\mathbb{E}[\text{Discount}] =1|𝒟discount|​∑δ∈𝒟discountδ\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{\text{discount}}|}\sum_{\delta\in\mathcal{D}_{\text{discount}}}\delta

For product weight, Jensen’s inequality implies 𝔼⁡[1/W]≠1/𝔼⁡[W]\mathbb{E}[1/W]\neq 1/\mathbb{E}[W]. The planner computes the expected inverse weight over non-zero domain entries:

𝔼⁡[1W]=1|𝒟W|​∑w∈𝒟W1w\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{W}\right]=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{D}_{W}|}\sum_{w\in\mathcal{D}_{W}}\frac{1}{w}

Optimization

At each chance node, an uninspected attribute kk can reveal any value x∈𝒟kx\in\mathcal{D}_{k}. When the cardinality of an empirical domain exceeds the chance enumeration limit (L=10L=10), the support is deterministically quantized into LL representative percentiles using evenly spaced indices:

ℐL={⌊i⋅(|𝒟k|−1)L−1⌋|i=0,…,L−1}\mathcal{I}_{L}=\left\{\left\lfloor\frac{i\cdot(|\mathcal{D}_{k}|-1)}{L-1}\right\rfloor\;\Bigg|\;i=0,\dots,L-1\right\}

Each quantized outcome x∈𝒟k​[ℐL]x\in\mathcal{D}_{k}[\mathcal{I}_{L}] is assigned an equal probability mass P⁡(x)=1/LP(x)=1/L.

The value of an information state V⁡(s,d)V(s,d) at remaining lookahead depth dd is governed by the Bellman optimality equation:

V(s,d)=max(maxj∈𝒥𝒰choose(j,s),𝕀(d>0)⋅max(reveal,j,k)∈𝒜reveal​(s)Qreveal(s,j,k,d))V(s,d)=\max\left(\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\mathcal{U}_{\text{choose}}(j,s),\quad\mathbb{I}(d>0)\cdot\max_{(\text{reveal},j,k)\in\mathcal{A}_{\text{reveal}}(s)}Q_{\text{reveal}}(s,j,k,d)\right)

where the Expected Value of Information for inspecting cell (j,k)(j,k) is computed across all chance outcomes Ω⁡(k)\Omega(k):

Qreveal(s,j,k,d)=1|Ω⁡(k)|∑x∈Ω⁡(k)V(s∪{(j,k)←x},d−1)Q_{\text{reveal}}(s,j,k,d)=\frac{1}{|\Omega(k)|}\sum_{x\in\Omega(k)}V\Big(s\cup\{(j,k)\leftarrow x\},\;d-1\Big)

We evaluate the normative policy under two planning horizons. The myopic policy (Depth=1\text{Depth}=1) values each possible acquisition as if it were the last before choosing. It therefore captures the value of an attribute on its own but not the value of attributes that are informative only in combination. The 2-step lookahead policy (Depth=2\text{Depth}=2) values each possible acquisition by also considering one further acquisition before choosing. It therefore captures complementarity between attributes, such as the cents of both alternatives, or a list price together with its discount percentage.

Under both horizons, the policy is recomputed after each acquisition from the updated information state. Ties between actions of equal value are broken at random, so each policy is simulated 100 times per cost condition.

Normative benchmark - Study 1

In Study 1, the ground-truth choice set pits a lower whole-dollar alternative (Coffee A: $4.99, 10.0 oz; 0.499 $/oz) against a higher whole-dollar optimal alternative (Coffee B: $5.00, 11.0 oz; 0.455 $/oz).

Table W41 summarizes the search depth and choice optimality of the Expectimax benchmark across acquisition costs.

Note. N=100N=100 independent simulations per cell. Ground truth realization: Coffee A ($4.99, 10 oz) vs. Coffee B ($5.00, 11 oz). Choice optimality is coded 1 if Coffee B is selected.

Given free acquisition (c=$0.00c=\$0.00) and small cost (c=$0.01c=\$0.01), both planning horizons acquire all 6 diagnostic cells (2 dollars, 2 cents, 2 weights) and choose optimally (100%100\%). Non-diagnostic cells are dropped immediately once cost rises to $0.01\$0.01 because their EVI is zero.

Under $10 cost, (c=$10.00c=\$10.00) search depth truncates to 3 tool calls (2 weights, 1 dollar). The 2-step planner halts search and satisfices on Coffee B (Optimality=1.00\text{Optimality}=1.00).

Normative benchmark - Study 2

In Study 2, the choice environment tests three alternatives where promotional cues and value point in opposing directions: Coffee C (lowest list price: $8.00, 0% discount, 8 oz; 1.00 $/oz), Coffee D (promotional cue: $15.00, 20% discount, 12 oz; 1.00 $/oz), and Coffee E (optimal unit price: $10.00, 0% discount, 10.9 oz; 0.917 $/oz).

Table W42 presents the search trajectories across costs.

Note. N=100N=100 independent simulations per cell. Ground truth realization: Coffee C ($8.00, 0%, 8 oz), Coffee D ($15.00, 20%, 12 oz), Coffee E ($10.00, 0%, 10.9 oz). Choice optimality is coded 1 if Coffee E is selected.

As cost increases from zero to $50, the optimal policies first truncate acquisition of discount percentage and then, under higher costs, list price and weight.

Normative benchmark - assigned information states

The exogenously assigned states of Web Appendix F present the surrogate consumer with a fixed subset of cells and no means of acquiring the remainder. The legal action space at such a state contains only choose actions, since 𝒜reveal​(s)=∅\mathcal{A}_{\text{reveal}}(s)=\varnothing by construction. The indicator on the reveal branch of the Bellman recursion is therefore never satisfied, and

V⁡(s,d)=maxj∈𝒥⁡𝒰choose​(j,s)V(s,d)=\max_{j\in\mathcal{J}}\mathcal{U}_{\text{choose}}(j,s)

for every dd. The value function is invariant to the planning horizon, and the myopic and 2-step lookahead policies coincide at every assigned state. The chance enumeration limit LL is likewise inoperative, since it governs the quantization of outcomes at reveal branches only. We accordingly report a single normative choice per state rather than one per planning horizon.

Because no inspections occur, Ctool​(s)=0C_{\text{tool}}(s)=0 at every assigned state. The terminal utility reduces to

𝒰choose(j,s)=−𝔼[Pj∣s]⋅𝔼[1Wj|s]\mathcal{U}_{\text{choose}}(j,s)=-\mathbb{E}[P_{j}\mid s]\cdot\mathbb{E}\left[\frac{1}{W_{j}}\;\Bigg|\;s\right]

evaluated over the empirical priors of the preceding section. Where weight is revealed, 𝔼⁡[1/Wj∣s]=1/Wj\mathbb{E}[1/W_{j}\mid s]=1/W_{j}; where it is withheld, the expected inverse weight over the empirical domain is 𝔼⁡[1/W]=0.400\mathbb{E}[1/W]=0.400, which is a common factor across alternatives and does not affect the ranking. Where the cents are withheld, 𝔼⁡[Cents]=52.93​¢\mathbb{E}[\text{Cents}]=52.93\textcent enters all alternatives equally; where the discount is withheld, 𝔼⁡[Discount]=20.0%\mathbb{E}[\text{Discount}]=20.0\% does the same. The whole-dollar price and the list price are revealed at every assigned state, so their priors never bind and the benchmark is insensitive to those two domains.

Note. Entries are −𝒰choose​(j,s)-\mathcal{U}_{\text{choose}}(j,s), the expected effective unit cost of each alternative given the revealed cells, in dollars per ounce. Lower values are preferred, and the normative choice is the alternative minimizing the entry in its row. Values are comparable within a row but not across rows: where weight is withheld, the entry is multiplied by 𝔼⁡[1/W]=0.400\mathbb{E}[1/W]=0.400, and where weight is revealed it is divided by the observed weight, so the two sets of rows are on different scales. Coffee C and Coffee D are exactly indifferent at the complete Study 2 state by construction, both at 1.0000, and both are inferior to Coffee E. The normative choice is invariant to the planning horizon at every state for the reason given above. State labels follow Table W33.

At three of the four Study 1 states and three of the five Study 2 states, the normative choice given the revealed cells is not the alternative with the superior price-per-ounce at the true attribute values. Selecting the lower whole-dollar alternative when the cents are withheld, or the lowest-list-price alternative when weight is withheld, is optimal conditional on the state while producing an economically inferior outcome. The two criteria are distinguished throughout Web Appendix F as state consistency and choice optimality respectively.

Web appendix I: LLM configurations

Experimental parameters and default decoding configuration

We retain the provider’s default decoding configuration because our estimand is the behavior of LLMs as deployed in realistic agentic settings. This choice is increasingly not ours to make, as in July 2026 Google deprecated sampling parameters (e.g., temperature, top-p, and top-k), with the API ignoring these parameters and rejecting them in future releases (Google, 2026). Anthropic has similarly deprecated custom sampling parameters (Anthropic, 2026). Therefore, throughout all studies reported in the paper, we have used the provider default sampling parameters.

Application programming interfaces and client libraries

All experimental queries were dispatched programmatically using official provider client libraries. Google Gemini models were accessed via the Google GenAI Python SDK (google-genai) utilizing the unified models.generate_content interface. OpenAI models were queried via the OpenAI Python SDK (openai) using the Responses interface (client.responses.create and client.responses.parse), which integrates structured output validation with native reasoning controls. Anthropic models were executed via the Anthropic Python SDK (anthropic) through the Messages API (client.messages.create).

Model identifiers, sampling parameters, and reasoning efforts

The experimental suite encompasses eight frontier models across three major families.

Google Gemini family. Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite (API model identifier gemini-3.5-flash-lite), Gemini 3.8 Flash (API model identifier gemini-3.8-flash), and Gemini 3.1 Pro (API model identifier gemini-3.1-pro-preview) were queried using standard provider defaults, including a default sampling temperature of T=1.0T=1.0 and nucleus sampling threshold of top-p=0.95p=0.95. Gemini 3.5 Flash Lite operates under default minimal thinking level, Gemini 3.8 Flash operates under default medium thinking level, and Gemini 3.1 Pro operates under default high thinking level.

OpenAI GPT-5.6 family. GPT-5.6 Luna (API model identifier gpt-5.6-luna), GPT-5.6 Terra (API model identifier gpt-5.6-terra), and GPT-5.6 Sol (API model identifier gpt-5.6-sol) were queried using default sampling parameters with temperature T=1.0T=1.0, top-p=1.0p=1.0, and null presence and frequency penalties. All three GPT-5.6 variants were executed under default medium reasoning effort (reasoning={“effort”: “medium”, “summary”: “auto”}), allowing internal chain-of-thought processing before emitting final choices.

Anthropic Claude family. Claude Sonnet 5 (API model identifier claude-sonnet-5) and Claude Opus 5 (API model identifier claude-opus-5) were evaluated using default generation parameters, comprising temperature T=1.0T=1.0, top-p=1.0p=1.0. Both Claude models operated under adaptive thinking mode (thinking={“type”: “adaptive”, “display”: “summarized”}) with default high reasoning effort allocation (output_config={“effort”: “high”}).

Output structure and replication controls

Across all discrete choice and interactive Tool-Lab experiments, outputs were constrained to valid JSON structures matching Pydantic schemas without restricting the internal latent sampling distribution. Because autoregressive sampling produces stochastic variation across independent queries at default temperature, each experimental cell was evaluated over 100 independent Monte Carlo sessions with zero state retention between trials.

Web appendix J: Software details

Parallel mediation models were estimated in R (version 4.6.1) using brms (Bürkner, 2017, version 2.23.0;) with the cmdstanr backend and Stan (version 2.39.0). Per LLM mediations were estimated using lavaan (version 0.6.21).

For the parallel mediations, we ran four chains of 4,000 iterations each with 1,000 warmup iterations, retaining 12,000 posterior draws, with adapt_delta set to .99 and maximum treedepth 12.
